strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important problem: generalization of human activity recognition to unseen activities, sensor placements and users without per-task retraining.

The pipeline is described in enough detail to be reimplemented: knowledge-base construction, placement-specific FAISS vector stores, class-wise retrieval with RRF, and full prompt templates for all four agents are provided in the appendix.

Evaluation is broad in coverage: 8 public benchmarks, 10 baselines from three families, plus ablations on retrieval, evidence pruning, prior-knowledge injection, and choice of retrieval embedder (DTW / Moment / Mantis), with retrieval latency reported.

Several design choices are well motivated and sensibly engineered: placement-specific databases, reciprocal rank fusion to combine sensors, class-balanced retrieval to avoid long-tail bias, and subject-held-out splits so that inference users are disjoint from the database.

The ablation results are internally consistent: removing retrieval (81.6 -> 71.8), removing pruning (81.6 -> 68.2), and removing prior knowledge (81.6 -> 63.4) all degrade performance in the expected direction.
weaknesses: The central 'true zero-shot' framing is not defensible as stated. The pair-wise feature-importance knowledge base and the class-wise feature-statistics table handed to the LLM contain per-activity labels and per-class mean/std of the exact candidate classes, built from labeled data of the same datasets. This is in-context supervised classification / nearest-prototype classification with hand-crafted features, not zero-shot recognition. Figure 1's 'True Zero-shot / No Task-specific Retraining' claim should be corrected, and 'zero-shot' should be replaced by something like 'training-free in-context classification with labeled statistics'.

The most obvious and most important baseline is missing: a plain classifier over the same hand-crafted feature pool using the same per-class statistics (nearest centroid, GMM, logistic regression, kNN), and 1-NN over the very vector database ZARA already builds. Since the LLM is handed exactly the class mean±std table, a nearest-centroid classifier is the natural competitor, and without it the contribution of the LLM agents relative to a classical classifier is unquantified. This is the decisive missing experiment; ZARA's own 'no retrieval' ablation (71.8%) is essentially that setup and is still competitive with several baselines.

Baseline results look implausibly weak and suggest misconfiguration. Gemini-text scores 26.5% on Opportunity, a 4-class problem (chance = 25%), and 24.2% on UCI-HAR, while ZARA with the *same* Gemini-2.0-Flash backbone reaches 92.5% and 90.0% on the same data. A 65-point gap from the same model on the same inputs is not credible without much stronger analysis of prompt/baseline configuration, and the paper acknowledges the raw-numeric prompt is hard for LLMs. The headline '2.53x over the strongest baseline' is also computed against a single overall baseline (UniMTS, 32.1 F1) rather than the strongest per-dataset baseline or a tuned baseline, and ratios of bounded F1 scores are a weak way to express improvement.

The comparison mixes incompatible regimes. IMUGPT, NormWear, UniMTS and the trained heads in Table 2 require training a classifier on the database split, so they are not zero-shot; conversely ImageBind/IMU2CLIP are single-sensor methods evaluated by reporting the best placement per dataset. This makes the 'zero-shot' comparison table difficult to interpret and inflates the apparent gap.

The interpretability claim, one of the paper's two headline contributions ('explainable HAR', 'clear reasoning', 'verifiable interpretability'), is completely unvalidated. There is no human evaluation of the rationales, no faithfulness measure (does the cited feature actually drive the decision?), no plausibility or consistency metric, and no measurement of whether explanations correlate with correctness. Only anecdotal examples in Figures 3 and 12 are shown.

Metric anomalies that warrant verification. Accuracy and macro F1 are equal to within 0.2 points on all eight datasets and exactly equal on three (92.5/92.5, 90.0/90.0, 97.1/97.1); the same near-identity recurs in Table 2. This is possible with class-balanced sampling only if predicted class distributions are also near-balanced, which would be a remarkable coincidence for an LLM agent. The paper should confirm the macro-F1 implementation and report per-class precision/recall. Relatedly, the 'upper bound' metric (fraction of queries whose pruned set contains the ground truth) is non-standard and its relation to accuracy is never established.

Statistical rigor is insufficient for the claims made. Test sets contain only ~190-288 windows per dataset, there is a single run per configuration, no confidence intervals, no significance tests, and no seed variation. Differences of 1-2 points (e.g., ZARA vs ZARA_Mantis vs ZARA_Moment-L; ZARA 81.6 vs DTW-retrieval 79.1) are well within sampling noise and should not be presented as rankings ('wins 4/8 in F1').

Reproducibility gaps. The code URL in the abstract is literally blank ('Our codes are available at .'). Knowledge-base construction depends on AutoGluon permutation-based feature ranking, which itself requires fitting models on labeled data, yet the paper never specifies which AutoGluon model, how cross-validation is performed, or how importance scores are aggregated; this also further undercuts the 'no task-specific training' claim. End-to-end reproducibility also depends on a proprietary API.

The evidence for generalization is weaker than claimed. The 'plug-and-play to new activity combinations' claim is not tested by any cross-dataset or unseen-activity-set experiment; every benchmark builds its knowledge base and vector database from the same dataset and label inventory it is evaluated on. A true zero-shot test (train KB/database on datasets A, evaluate on unseen activities from dataset B) is absent, and near-duplicate windows from seen subjects in the vector database (10s windows, 2.5s windows, overlapping activities) are not analyzed for leakage effects.

No failure analysis. USC-HAD (60.0%) and WISDM (65.6%) are far below the other datasets, and per-class accuracy in Figure 8 shows near-zero performance on several classes (e.g., 'Kicking Ball' 6.2%, 'Folding Clothes' 31.2%, 'Elevator Down' 30.0%), yet the paper does not analyze why the agent fails or what this implies for the proposed reasoning mechanism.

Limited relevance to the ACL audience as presented: the NLP content is essentially RAG + prompting + RRF, with no analysis of explanation quality, no linguistic evaluation, and no methodological advance in language processing. The paper would need either a genuine interpretability evaluation or a stronger NLP-facing contribution to justify main-conference consideration.

strengths: The paper tackles a practical and important problem: training-free/zero-shot human activity recognition from raw motion time-series, with potential applications in wearable sensing and ubiquitous computing.

It proposes a well-engineered pipeline combining an automatically derived pair-wise feature-importance knowledge base, class-wise multi-sensor retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion, and hierarchical LLM-agent reasoning.
The experimental effort is substantial: 8 HAR benchmarks, 10 baselines, several ablations, detailed preprocessing descriptions, prompt templates, and per-class results.
The architecture is clearly presented, and the ablations provide useful evidence that retrieval, evidence pruning, and prior knowledge injection each contribute to performance.
The reported results, if taken at face value, show large improvements over the compared zero-shot baselines, and the method avoids fine-tuning or training task-specific classifiers.
weaknesses: The central 'zero-shot' claim is misleading: the method requires labeled data for all target activity classes to build class-wise retrieval databases and the pair-wise feature knowledge base. At inference, it assumes a known candidate activity set (or retrieves a top-10 candidate set), so it is not zero-shot in the standard sense of recognizing unseen activity classes. It is better described as supervised cross-subject retrieval/classification without task-specific fine-tuning.

The baseline comparisons are confounded and likely unfair. ZARA uses labeled data from seen subjects for retrieval and knowledge construction, whereas many baselines (e.g., HARGPT, Gemini text/plot/table, ImageBind, IMU2CLIP, NormWear, UniMTS) do not receive comparable supervised information. In addition, ZARA uses Gemini 2.0-Flash while HARGPT and IMUGPT use GPT-4o-mini, so model capability is entangled with method design.

The interpretability/explainability claim is not evaluated. The paper repeatedly promises verifiable, human-readable rationales, but there is no human evaluation, faithfulness metric, or analysis of explanation quality; only final classification metrics are reported.

Reproducibility is weak. The code URL is missing, the method relies on a proprietary LLM API, and there is no reporting of token usage, monetary cost, or LLM inference latency. The claim of deterministic outputs is not supported with multiple runs or statistical tests.

There is no analysis of intermediate-stage errors or error propagation in the hierarchical agent pipeline. It is unclear how much the LLM contributes beyond the retrieval and feature-statistics components, and no ablation isolates the LLM's reasoning from the retrieval classifier.

The paper lacks statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance estimates across seeds/LLM calls, despite making SOTA and 'first' claims that depend on small differences and API-based models.

The work has limited relevance to computational linguistics and NLP. The task is sensor-based human activity recognition, not language processing; the contribution is primarily to ubiquitous computing/wearable sensing, with language models used only as reasoning components over numeric time-series.

Some claims are overstated: 'first agent-based framework' and 'SOTA zero-shot' are not convincingly established given the non-zero-shot evaluation setting, the unequal supervision, and the lack of comparison to strong supervised baselines under identical conditions.

The evaluation samples class-balanced held-out sets per activity, which is not a realistic open-world deployment scenario. This further undermines the claimed plug-and-play zero-shot capability and may inflate accuracy.

strengths: Targets a practically important problem — cross-subject, classifier-free human activity recognition with natural-language justifications — and delivers a complete, end-to-end system (automatic knowledge base, placement-specific vector stores, class-wise RRF retrieval, and a four-stage LLM agent pipeline) rather than a partial prototype.

Empirical coverage is substantial: 8 public HAR datasets spanning easy/medium/hard difficulty, 10 baselines from three families (text-LLM, multimodal-LLM, pretrained HAR models), plus four ablations (retrieval on/off, evidence pruning, prior knowledge, retrieval-encoder choice) supported by a sensible upper-bound diagnostic that measures whether the pruned candidate set still contains the gold label.

The pair-wise Activity-Pair Feature Importance knowledge base is built automatically via AutoGluon permutation ranking with cross-validation, removing manual feature curation and making the knowledge label-inventory-agnostic; this is a clean, reusable design idea.

Reproducibility of the reasoning stage is reasonably well supported: full system and user prompt templates for all four agents (first/second Feature Selector, Evidence Pruning, Decision Insight) are provided, temperature is fixed at 0, and retrieval latency for four encoders is benchmarked on specified hardware.

The paper is generally well written and well organized, with informative figures (architecture, agent workflow, subject-split protocol) and a clear presentation of per-class results and dataset characteristics.
weaknesses: The 'zero-shot' framing is misleading and is never actually tested. The candidate activity list is supplied at inference, and the knowledge base and vector database contain labeled windows for every test class (drawn from held-out subjects). The protocol is therefore cross-subject, closed-set, classifier-free generalization — not zero-shot recognition of unseen activities. Yet the introduction claims the LLM 'can reason effectively about unseen activities', and the title/abstract foreground 'zero-shot'. No experiment with an entirely unseen activity class is reported, so the generality claim is unsupported as stated.

The headline '2.53x macro-F1 improvement over the strongest baseline' (Table 1) is an unfair comparison: ZARA uses target-class labeled support data for its knowledge base and retrieval index, while UniMTS, ImageBind, IMU2CLIP and the prompt-only LLMs use none. The only apples-to-apples comparison is Table 2, where ZARA beats Mantis with a trained classifier head by roughly 2.6 F1 points (92.5 vs 89.9). The abstract's framing overstates the contribution relative to the fair comparison.

A critical baseline is missing: no simple non-parametric classifier (nearest-class-mean, k-NN, or an SVM on the same handcrafted features and class-wise statistics) is evaluated. Because the Decision Insight agent essentially compares query features against per-class mean±std tables, a nearest-class-mean model on the same features could plausibly match ZARA. Without this control, it is impossible to attribute performance to the LLM agents rather than to the feature/statistics pipeline, which undercuts the central claim of the paper's title.

The interpretability claim is asserted but not evaluated. The abstract and contributions promise 'concise, verifiable rationales' and 'human-readable explanations', and Figure 1 lists 'Textual Explanations' as a differentiator from baselines, yet no human study, faithfulness metric, or even a sample rationale from the main experiments is reported. 'Verifiable' is used without any verification.

The efficiency argument is not substantiated. The abstract criticizes prior LLM approaches for excessive token usage and high cost, but ZARA issues four sequential LLM calls per query in addition to retrieval over the full candidate set. Only retrieval latency is reported (Table 6); LLM token consumption and end-to-end latency per query are never measured, so the efficiency advantage is unsupported.

Evaluation is based on small, sampled subsets (roughly 190-288 windows per dataset) with no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Given this sample size, several reported differences (between ZARA variants, and ZARA vs. Mantis) may not be statistically meaningful, and the near-identical performance of ZARA_DTW (90.5), ZARA_Moment (91.0) and ZARA_Mantis (92.5) suggests the retrieval encoder contributes little.

Baseline reproduction choices may systematically disadvantage competitors: HARGPT and IMUGPT are run with GPT-4o-mini rather than the GPT-4 used in the original HARGPT work, and several baselines are re-implemented with bespoke prompt templates and downsampling. This inflates the apparent gap and makes the cross-method numbers hard to interpret.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code link is blank ('Our codes are available at .'), key hyperparameters such as TOP_N, the number of selected features m/n, and knowledge-base construction details are only partially specified, and results depend on a proprietary, nondeterministic LLM API (Gemini-2.0-flash).

Relevance to ACL is borderline. The contribution is primarily an application of RAG plus multi-agent prompting to wearable-sensor time series; the NLP methodology (statistics tables in the prompt, RRF retrieval, agent chaining) is a fairly standard pattern, so the paper's core novelty for the computational-linguistics community is limited and might be better suited to a ubiquitous-computing venue.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem—training-free adaptation of HAR systems—and proposes a coherent pipeline combining statistical knowledge distillation, retrieval, and hierarchical LLM agents.

The method is technically well designed and clearly described: pairwise feature-importance profiling, placement-specific vector stores, class-wise multi-sensor retrieval, RRF fusion, and staged agent reasoning are all specified in detail.

The empirical study is extensive, covering 8 HAR benchmarks, 10 baselines, cross-subject and cross-dataset evaluations, plus ablations on retrieval, evidence pruning, prior knowledge, token usage, and latency.
Ablations convincingly show that retrieval, evidence pruning, and injected prior knowledge each materially improve performance, supporting the core architectural choices.

ZARA is competitive with or superior to strong supervised baselines on several datasets (Table 2), and the paper is transparent about limitations, including reliance on a labeled retrieval database and higher inference cost.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed appendix material, including prompt templates, feature definitions, preprocessing steps, and dataset statistics.
weaknesses: The "training-free" framing is overstated: ZARA still requires a labeled support set to build the retrieval database and uses AutoGluon to fit feature-importance models. Comparing against baselines without access to this labeled target-domain support set is not fully apples-to-apples, so the very large margins in Table 1 may partly reflect extra supervision rather than training-free generalization alone.

Cross-dataset generalization is only partially demonstrated: the retrieval database is constructed from the target domain, so only the feature-importance knowledge is transferred. The paper does not include external baselines in the cross-dataset setting, weakening the claim of robust cross-domain transfer.

The interpretability claim is not empirically evaluated. The generated rationales are not assessed for faithfulness, correctness, or utility, and no human study or rationale-quality metric is reported.

There is no simple non-LLM retrieval baseline (e.g., k-NN over frozen embeddings or a feature-based classifier) to isolate how much of the gain comes from the LLM agent rather than from retrieval and statistical comparison alone.

Results are reported without error bars or statistical significance tests, and inference is run at temperature 0 on sampled test subsets. This makes it difficult to judge the stability of the reported gains, especially for smaller benchmarks.

Relevance to computational linguistics and NLP is limited: the core task is sensor-based human activity recognition rather than language processing, and the NLP contribution is largely an application of existing LLM/RAG techniques to numerical time-series.
Some important recent methods are not compared due to modality mismatch, and the code link in the abstract is missing/blank, which limits the paper's immediate reproducibility and positioning.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in human activity recognition: generalization to unseen subjects/domains, interpretability, and adaptation without model fine-tuning. The motivation is clearly articulated and well supported by prior-work discussion.

Introduces a novel and coherent framework that decouples universal knowledge (pairwise feature-importance priors distilled from statistics) from local evidence (retrieval over labeled sensor windows), and combines both with a hierarchical multi-agent LLM workflow.

Empirical evaluation is extensive: 8 HAR datasets, 10 baselines, multiple LLM backbones, cross-subject and cross-dataset settings, and detailed ablations of retrieval, evidence pruning, and prior knowledge. The gains over training-free baselines are large and consistent.

Ablation studies are informative and well executed. Removing retrieval, evidence pruning, or prior knowledge each causes substantial drops, demonstrating that all components contribute to the final performance.

The paper is reproducible and transparent: code is provided (anonymized), prompts are included in full in the appendix, dataset preprocessing and subject splits are detailed, token usage and latency are reported, and temperature is set to 0 for deterministic inference.

The agent workflow is interpretable by design and produces evidence-backed rationales. The textual knowledge base is human-readable, and the prompts require the model to justify predictions against statistical feature distributions.

Relevant to ACL/LLM audiences interested in tool use, retrieval-augmented reasoning, and grounding language models in non-text modalities. The method shows that LLM agents can reason over motion time-series when provided with structured, statistically grounded textual evidence.
weaknesses: The 'training-free' framing is somewhat overstated: the method requires a labeled support set/reference database to build the retrieval index and prior knowledge base. This is not zero-shot label-free adaptation, even though no model parameters are updated. The limitation is acknowledged in the Limitations section, but the title and abstract should better reflect this requirement.

The cross-dataset generalization claim is weakened by the fact that the retrieval database is constructed from the target domain. The experiments therefore test transferability of motion priors, not label-free generalization to a new dataset. The source knowledge helps, but target-domain labels are still required for retrieval.

Baseline fairness is a concern. ZARA is given a labeled retrieval support set and pairwise feature-importance knowledge, while most training-free baselines are not. Some baselines are adapted from single-sensor settings and may be under-tuned for multi-sensor HAR. The very large gaps may partly reflect the experimental setup rather than purely the proposed method.

No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported. Inference sets are small random subsets (roughly 190–288 samples per dataset) due to API cost, which limits comparability to full benchmarks and makes it difficult to assess the reliability of small differences.

Interpretability is claimed as a key benefit, but there is no quantitative or human evaluation of the generated rationales. It is unclear whether the explanations are faithful to the model’s internal decision process or useful to human users.

Inference cost is high. Input token usage can reach around 17k tokens per query, and the pipeline uses multiple LLM calls per prediction. This limits practical scalability, especially for real-time or on-device HAR applications.

The method’s sensitivity to prompt design and LLM backbone is not deeply analyzed. Ablations and cross-dataset experiments use only Gemini-2.0-Flash, so it is unclear how robust the framework is across different LLMs or prompt paraphrases.

Some experimental details are unclear, particularly the exact subject splits and overlap avoidance in the cross-dataset setting. A clearer statement of whether retrieval and inference windows come from disjoint subjects is needed to rule out potential data leakage.

Recent LLM/sensor methods such as SensorLM, LLaSA, and RelCon are not directly compared due to modality mismatch. This is understandable, but it leaves the positioning relative to the most closely related recent work somewhat incomplete.

strengths: The problem is well motivated and the core intuition is sound: rather than projecting raw sensor streams into an LLM, the paper translates implicit signal statistics into explicit textual priors (pairwise feature-importance profiles) and pairs them with local, placement-specific retrieval. The decoupling of 'universal knowledge' from 'local evidence' is a clean and reusable design idea.

The system is described with reasonable clarity (architecture figure, four-stage agent workflow, explicit prompt templates in Appendix A.7), and the engineering effort is substantial: 8 HAR benchmarks, 10 baselines, 4 LLM backbones, retrieval-backbone ablations, and supporting analyses of token usage, retrieval latency and per-class behaviour.

The ablations are informative and internally consistent: removing retrieval (81.6 -> 71.8), removing the pruning agent (81.6 -> 68.2) and removing the prior knowledge base (81.6 -> 63.4) each produce large, directionally sensible degradations, which supports the claim that the injected statistical priors do real work.

The paper is relatively candid in places: it reports the frozen-encoder + supervised-head comparison (Table 2), acknowledges that a labeled retrieval database is still required (Limitations), and does not hide the fact that the cross-dataset knowledge setting sometimes underperforms in-dataset knowledge.
weaknesses: The central 'training-free' framing is misleading and makes the headline comparison (Table 1) not apples-to-apples. ZARA consumes labeled in-domain data twice over: the retrieval vector store is built from seen subjects of the target dataset, and the pairwise feature-importance knowledge base is derived from labeled activity windows. The zero-shot baselines it is compared against (UniMTS, ImageBind, IMU2CLIP, HARGPT) use no target-domain labels. The honest comparison class is a frozen encoder plus a classifier trained on the same support split.

By that honest comparison the SOTA claim collapses: the paper's own Table 2 shows a frozen Mantis encoder with a supervised head averaging ~82.7% accuracy versus ZARA's 81.6%, i.e., ZARA roughly matches a far cheaper baseline while requiring multi-agent LLM calls on every query. The abstract's 'state-of-the-art performance in parameter-frozen settings' is therefore not supported; the claim should be reframed as parity with supervised frozen-encoder baselines at substantially higher inference cost.

The 40-point gap to the pretrained baselines is more plausibly a protocol artifact than a capability difference. ImageBind and IMU2CLIP are forced into fixed 6x2000 single-sensor windows via repeat-padding/interpolation, HARGPT/Gemini are prompted with different input modalities, and no tuning of the class-text prompts for UniMTS is reported. No evidence is given that these baselines were given a fair shot at the HAR task.

There is essentially no statistical rigor. Inference sets are tiny (190-288 class-balanced windows per dataset) and randomly subsampled, no random seeds are reported, no confidence intervals or significance tests are given, and class-balanced sampling inflates accuracy relative to the natural label distribution. Many of the reported margins (and much of the cross-dataset analysis in Figure 5) are within noise.

Interpretability and 'evidence-grounded rationales' are advertised as one of three contributions, yet the generated rationales are never evaluated. There is no faithfulness analysis, no human evaluation, no error taxonomy, and no check that the cited features actually drove the prediction. 'Trustworthy' and 'transparent' remain assertions rather than demonstrated properties.

The per-class evidence contradicts the paper's own text. Figure 9 shows several classes at 0-20% accuracy (e.g., Elevator Up 0.0%, Eating Sandwich 8.2%, Cycling variants 0.0% on DSADS), yet Section A.5 states ZARA 'consistently achieves strong per-class performance' and 'balanced generalization'. The discrepancy is not discussed.

The cross-dataset transfer story is overstated. In Figure 5, cross-dataset knowledge beats in-dataset knowledge in only 3 of 8 transfers and frequently fails to beat the no-knowledge control; the abstract's 'strong transferability across heterogeneous sensor domains' is not what the figure shows. Similarly, the 'open-set' framing is undercut by class-wise retrieval that presupposes a candidate activity list.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract literally ends with 'Our code is available at .', no seeds or sampling procedures are pinned down, key hyperparameters (TOP_N, the number of coarse/fine features, pruning thresholds, RRF constants beyond k=60) are unspecified, and the evaluation depends on random subsampling that cannot be replicated exactly.

The cost argument is asserted rather than demonstrated. Only retrieval latency is reported (Table 9); the end-to-end latency, API cost and failure rate of the four-stage agentic pipeline are never compared against the supervised frozen-encoder baseline or against the LLM baselines whose token cost ZARA criticizes. For a paper claiming a 'plug-and-play alternative to training-intensive pipelines', this is a decisive missing analysis.

Relevance to ACL is thin: the technical ingredients (handcrafted time/frequency features, AutoGluon permutation importance, RRF fusion, prompted LLM agents) are all off-the-shelf, and the contribution is an application-domain combination rather than a methodological insight about language, reasoning or retrieval. There is little that a computational-linguistics audience could transfer beyond the specific HAR pipeline.
